title: LIBS 7102 · Lecture 1
subtitle: Foundations of ethical debate: philosophy and the three branches of ethics, valid and sound arguments, empirical, value and conceptual claims, trick questions, and genuine moral action
description: Lecture 1 of LIBS 7102 Ethics for Computing Professionals: what philosophy does that science cannot; meta-, normative and applied ethics; no ought without can, no ought from is, explanation is not justification; arguments, premises and conclusions, and why an argument is never true or false; deductive and inductive arguments; validity, soundness and the slide's practice arguments; empirical, value and conceptual claims and the value-argument shape; the trick questions the exam uses; Gyges' ring, psychological and normative egoism, Hume and Williams on why genuine moral action exists. Ends with a 20-item mock quiz.
intro:
:::exam Midterm facts
**Midterm: Wednesday Oct 28, in class.** Closed book, two hours, on paper, 20 % of the course. You write four or five two-paragraph answers, choosing from about six (for example, answer 4 of 6). Questions cover lectures 1 to 5 and are taken from the practice list (rare) or very similar to it (typical), often paired with a computing case or asking you to argue a side. It feeds the moral-reasoning question that most midterms include, which scores close to 100 % or 0 %.
:::

lessons.title: Philosophy asks what science cannot answer, and ethics has three branches
Valid means the premises guarantee the conclusion; sound adds true premises
Validity drill: judge each argument valid or invalid, sound or unsound
Claims are empirical, value or conceptual, and a value conclusion needs a value premise
Some exam tasks cannot be done, and the answer says why
Self-interest is not selfishness, so genuine moral action exists
